lines.text: Rainforest temples, volcanoes and a people who never forgot their Maya roots. This is the story of Guatemala, from Tikal to today.
Deep in the northern jungle, around 600 BCE, the Maya built El Mirador, one of their first great cities, with pyramids among the largest ever raised.
Soon Tikal rose too, its temple pyramids climbing above the trees. For more than a thousand years its kings fought and traded with rival cities, until it was abandoned.
In 1524 the Spanish arrived and began their conquest. The region's capital moved more than once before settling at Guatemala City, now the largest city in Central America.
For two centuries Spain ruled from Antigua, a graceful colonial capital, until earthquakes left it in ruins.
In the 1500s the Kiche Maya wrote down their sacred book, the Popol Vuh, the tale of the hero twins and of people made from maize.
In 1821, after three centuries of Spanish rule, Guatemala declared its independence, and soon stood as a nation of its own.
By 1899 the American United Fruit Company was at work, owning vast banana lands, railways and ports, and holding great sway over the government.
That same year Miguel Angel Asturias was born, the novelist who would win the Nobel Prize in 1967.
Juan Jose Arevalo, born in 1904, would become the first freely elected president in 1945.
His successor would be Jacobo Arbenz, whose land reform took unused land from great estates, including those of United Fruit.
Efrain Rios Montt, born in 1926, would rule as a general in the early eighties. Decades later, a Guatemalan court convicted him of genocide against the Maya.
In 1954 a coup backed by the CIA overthrew Arbenz, and Guatemala's experiment with democracy came to an end.
Bernardo Arevalo, son of the first elected president, was born in 1958. In 2024 he too would become president.
A year later came Rigoberta Menchu, a Kiche woman who would tell the world of her people's suffering and win the Nobel Peace Prize.
From the early sixties, the country sank into civil war. By the peace of 1996, some two hundred thousand people had died, most of them Maya.
In the middle of the war, in 1976, a great earthquake killed some twenty-three thousand people.
And in 2018 the Volcan de Fuego erupted, its burning flows burying villages on its slopes.
Through conquest, war, earthquake and fire, Guatemala and its Maya heart still endure.
